To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
negative pretraining is an important phenomenon that can occur when a pretrained neural network model is trained on a target learning task.

(1) a pretrained network can obtain a worse generalization error than one trained from scratch on the target task, (2) this is due to a combination of the pretraining task and the target task, and (3) the effect can be fixed by changing either the learning rate or the network architecture

negative pretraining can be removed by: 1) altering learning rates after pretraining, 2) increasing the discretization between pretraining and the target task, or 3) resetting network biases to a large value.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: How does a neural network’s pretraining on one dataset impact the final generalization performance of a network on a target dataset?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

negative pretraining is an effect where the performance of a model trained from scratch on a target task can outperform a model that is pre-trained on a source task, and then fine-tuned on the target task.
negative pretraining effects are caused by the fact that a model trained on a source task is already in a state of local minimum.

the negative pretraining is a problem that is very much dependent on the task at hand and on the architecture of the network, and that it can be solved by a number of different methods, which all seem to be related to the fact that the pretraining is too specific for the target task and that the network has to forget some of this information to generalize better to the target task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the negative pretraining is a phenomenon that can be fixed by changing the learning rate, the learning task and the model architecture.

we show that the negative pretraining phenomenon is not just a problem for the pretraining process itself but rather a problem for the entire learning pipeline and that we provide three ways to fix it.

negative pretraining is a real phenomenon, and it is not necessarily a problem, but rather a consequence of the learning dynamics of the network, which can be fixed with the right set of interventions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
negative pretraining can be removed with a few simple interventions, and that it may be more important to understand the learning process than the task or the model.
pretraining can be a useful technique, but only when used correctly and with care.
pretraining is a complex process that can be improved with careful tuning of the pretraining and learning process.
